accepted.question_text: In gamma-ray burst (GRB) studies, bursts have traditionally been classified as long/soft or short/hard using the duration measure T90, with about 2 seconds as a rough dividing line, together with spectral hardness. Because T90 depends on detector bandpass and sensitivity and does not always track the physical origin of a burst, what classification scheme should be used to map observed GRBs to physically meaningful progenitor classes such as massive-star (Type II) events versus compact-object-merger (Type I) events?

evidence.quote: The main issue of applying the T90 criterion to define the class of a GRB is that T90 is detector dependent.
This suggests that certain observation properties (e.g. long vs. short duration) do not always refer to certain types of progenitor.

accepted.question_text: What progenitor systems actually produce the main classes of gamma-ray bursts? More specifically, which stellar or compact-object channels generate massive-star GRBs and compact-star GRBs, given that current evidence is indirect, only a small and biased subset of long GRBs have secure supernova associations, and some short-duration or high-redshift events do not fit a simple neutron-star-merger picture?

evidence.quote: The progenitors of GRBs are not identified, and it will be very difficult to identify them.
Despite the indirect supports to the merger scenarios mentioned above, following observational facts raise cautions to take the merger progenitors as truth.

accepted.question_text: Which central engine powers gamma-ray bursts in nature: a black-hole-plus-accretion-torus system, a rapidly spinning highly magnetized neutron star (magnetar), or a quark star, and what observational diagnostic can distinguish these engine models uniquely? Any answer must account for the fact that a GRB engine has to launch extremely luminous, highly relativistic, baryon-clean, collimated, variable, and sometimes long-lasting outflows.

evidence.quote: Since all three types of engine are argued to satisfy most observational constraints, identifying the right one among them using observational data is not straightforward.
Unfortunately, besides theoretical arguments, there is essentially no “smoking-gun” observational criterion to differentiate a QS engine from a NS engine.

accepted.question_text: What is the composition of gamma-ray-burst ejecta at the prompt-emission radius: are the outflows primarily matter-dominated fireballs or magnetically dominated jets, and what are the baryon, lepton-pair, and neutron contents of the flow? Here the key quantity is the magnetization sigma, the ratio of Poynting flux to matter flux, and the problem is to determine whether sigma is much less than 1, of order 1, or much greater than 1 in the emitting region.

evidence.quote: Diagnosing the composition of GRB ejecta has not been an easy task.
To summarize, the case of GRB composition is inconclusive.

accepted.question_text: What physical process dissipates the energy of a gamma-ray-burst outflow and accelerates the radiating particles above the photosphere? In particular, are the dominant mechanisms internal or external shocks, magnetic reconnection in a Poynting-flux-dominated flow, turbulence-driven reconnection, or direct electromagnetic acceleration, and under what conditions can these mechanisms efficiently accelerate particles in highly magnetized plasma?

evidence.quote: Whether and how particles are accelerated in magnetized shocks is subject to more investigations.
Particle acceleration in such turbulence-reconnection events is a difficult problem.

accepted.question_text: What radiation mechanism produces the prompt gamma-ray-burst spectrum that is usually fit by the empirical Band function? The unresolved possibilities include synchrotron or jitter emission from accelerated leptons, synchrotron self-Compton emission, Comptonization of thermal or photospheric photons, and hadronic emission, and the explanation must account for observed low-energy spectral slopes, cooling behavior, and peak energies.

evidence.quote: While the origin of the external shock afterglow is relatively well modeled … the radiation mechanism of the prompt GRB emission is subject to debate.
It is difficult to identify the correct radiation mechanism with the current available data.

accepted.question_text: Why does the gamma-ray-burst central engine remain active after the initial prompt burst, producing late-time X-ray flares and X-ray plateaus that are often too rapid or too steep to arise from an external shock alone? What physical mechanism—such as fallback accretion, magnetar spin-down, disk fragmentation, magnetic barriers, post-merger magnetic activity, or quark-star activity—can explain both the long duration and the erratic behavior of this late central-engine emission?

evidence.quote: One of the major discoveries of Swift is that the so-called “afterglow” is not only the emission from the external shock … but also includes emission from a long-lasting central engine.
There is no well accepted mechanism yet to account for the erratic behavior of the late central engine activities.

accepted.question_text: Which components of observed post-burst gamma-ray-burst light curves are genuinely produced by the external forward or reverse shock, and how should jet breaks, chromatic behavior, and reverse-shock signatures be interpreted once internal central-engine contributions are removed? This is especially important in the Swift era, where X-ray afterglows commonly contain multiple components that complicate standard external-shock parameter inference.

evidence.quote: Therefore, in the Swift era, the afterglow modeling made one step backwards: instead of constraining the afterglow model parameters using the data, one needs first to identify which emission component is from the external forward shock, and which is not.
There is no platinum jet breaks identified (i.e. those clearly show achromatic feature in all wavelengths).

accepted.question_text: What produces gamma-ray-burst emission above 100 MeV, especially the frequent delay of Large Area Telescope (LAT) photons relative to the lower-energy prompt emission, the long-lived GeV decay phase, and the varying spectral relation between the GeV and MeV bands? The explanation must determine whether the high-energy signal is internal, external-shock afterglow emission, or a superposition of multiple components.

evidence.quote: Even though the origin of high energy emission is still subject to debate, these new data shed light into several open questions in GRB prompt emission physics…
This suggests either that the entire high energy emission has a different origin from the MeV emission … or that the high energy lightcurve is the superposition of two components…

accepted.question_text: Are massive-star gamma-ray bursts reliable tracers of the star-formation history of the universe across cosmic time, especially at high redshift?

evidence.quote: Are massive star GRBs good tracers of star formation history of the universe?

accepted.question_text: Do massive-star gamma-ray bursts preferentially occur in low-metallicity environments, and is such a metallicity bias needed to explain the observed high-redshift GRB event rate?

evidence.quote: Do these GRBs favor a low metallicity environment?
One therefore needs to argue that GRBs favor low metallicity environment [54,335,336,337] or their luminosity function evolves with redshift so that luminosity is higher at higher-z.

accepted.question_text: Does the luminosity function of gamma-ray bursts evolve with redshift or cosmic time, so that bursts at higher redshift are systematically more luminous than those nearby?

evidence.quote: Does the GRB luminosity function evolve with time?
One therefore needs to argue that GRBs favor low metallicity environment [54,335,336,337] or their luminosity function evolves with redshift so that luminosity is higher at higher-z.

accepted.question_text: Can high-redshift gamma-ray bursts be used to probe the reionization history of the universe through their near-infrared afterglow spectra, thereby constraining how and when cosmic reionization occurred?

evidence.quote: Can high-z GRBs probe the reionization history of the universe?
As bright beacons in the “dark ages”, these high-z GRBs can probe the cosmic reionization history in their near IR afterglow spectrum.

accepted.question_text: Do gamma-ray bursts at very high redshift arise from progenitors different from those of lower-redshift bursts, for example from an earlier stellar population that forms more massive stars and perhaps powers more energetic events?

evidence.quote: Do high-z GRBs have a different progenitor from the low-z ones?
The first generation stars may be more massive than the nearby massive stars [344].
